rules_text:
Rules summary Resolve is a connection game for two players, Black and White, with sufficient black and white stones. Starting with Black, players take turns placing and swapping stones on the intersecting points of a square grid (with side lengths of either 5, 9, 13, or 19) which is initially empty. Passing is forbidden. Same-colored stones with orthogonal adjacency are connected. The game is over when a player wins by connecting their designated sides of the board with a single group of connected stones of their color, at any time during their turn or their opponent's turn. Cutting stones are four stones in the following generic crosscut configuration: OX XO On your turn, place a stone of your color on an empty point, if possible. If that created a crosscut, swap the placed stone with different adjacent enemy stones that share a crosscut with it, until that stone is no longer part of a crosscut. If you haven't placed a stone this turn, then instead choose a friendly stone in a crosscut and resolve as above.

[Rating: 6/10] In this game you are trying to connect your stones from one of your colored sides to the other.  The key is "resoolving" crosscuts.

[Rating: 7/10] Decent game, but I prefer Reneo, a similar game that fixes some issues I have with Resolve. Unlike Resolve, Reneo is free of chain reactions and cycles. Also, in Resolve, some crosscuts are unresolvable until the board is full, and the second player (on odd-sized boards) or the first player (on even-sized boards) is guaranteed to be the first to solve one of those sticky crosscuts. Reneo avoids this by ensuring that there are no crosscuts on the board at the end of any turn.

[Rating: 9/10] Connecting opposite sides of a square with an orthogonal path is usually an impossible task, as the opponents can block each other with crosscuts. Several solutions to this problem has been offered -- most famously, John Nash has proven  that a similar game on a hexagonal board will be drawless.   Alek's solution is surprizing -- whenever a crosscut arizes, the players can choose to resolve it performing a special "swap" move partially inspired by Slyde. This makes the game more dynamic than your standard issue placement games, as the board is prone to dramatic changes in span of few moves.  B
